opus-5.5.text:
I think representation is really the core of the whole thing, and honestly it's the part that gets underestimated the most right now.

When people talk about world models today, a lot of the attention goes to generation: can you produce a beautiful video, can you roll out the next few seconds of a scene with high fidelity. That's impressive, but I don't think pixel-level generation by itself is the goal. A world model is supposed to help an agent understand, predict, and eventually act. For that, what matters is whether the model has formed a good internal representation of the world: objects, space, geometry, physics, causality. Pixels are just the surface.

So in terms of architecture, I see representation as the backbone that everything else sits on. You have an encoder that maps raw observations into some latent space. You have a predictive or dynamics component that operates in that space. Then, optionally, you have a decoder if you want to render things back out. If the latent space is poor, if it's only capturing low-level texture statistics, then no matter how powerful your dynamics model or decoder is, you're building on sand. The model might look like it understands the world because the videos look plausible, but it hasn't actually abstracted anything.

We've seen evidence of this in our own work. For example, when we started aligning the internal features of diffusion models with strong pretrained visual representations, training became much faster and the quality got better. That told us something important. Generative models, left alone, are spending a huge amount of capacity just rediscovering representations that self-supervised learning already knows how to learn. Generation and representation shouldn't be two separate worlds. Good representation makes generation easier, and generation can be one signal for learning representation, but it shouldn't be the only one.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that representation for world models has to go beyond what we've traditionally done in vision. A lot of visual representation learning has been about 2D images, recognition, classification, semantics. A world model needs spatial intelligence. It needs to understand 3D structure, how things persist when they're occluded, how they move, what happens when you interact with them. Even today's strongest multimodal models are surprisingly weak at basic spatial reasoning. To me that's a sign that the representations underneath are still missing something fundamental.

So my view is that the field needs to put representation learning back at the center. Not as an old-fashioned pretraining stage you do once and forget, but as the main design question: what should the latent space of a world model look like, what should it be predictive of, and how do we learn it from rich, continuous, embodied sensory experience instead of just text or static images. If we get that right, I think the generation, planning, and action parts will follow much more naturally.

r001.rationale: It calls representation “the core” and “the backbone” of a world model, and says representation learning should be the main design question.

r002.rationale: It describes a latent representation and an optional decoder for rendering, but does not say the shared representation can be decoded into different output modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think representation is actually the thing people have been underestimating in this whole world model conversation. Right now a lot of the field treats world modeling as basically a generation problem, and the dominant recipe is something like a video diffusion model or a big autoregressive model trained on raw pixels, and you hope that if the model can predict the next frame well enough, understanding of the world will emerge along the way. And I'm honestly skeptical of that framing, or at least I think it's incomplete.

My view is that the representation is where the actual "world" in the world model lives. Pixels are not the right currency for physics, for causality, for object permanence, for the intentions of an agent. Those things exist at a level of abstraction above pixels. So if your architecture forces the model to spend most of its capacity reconstructing texture and lighting, you're paying a very large tax for something that has nothing to do with understanding how the world works. We've seen this in our own work, where if you take a generative model and look inside it, the internal features are often quite a bit weaker than what you get from a good self-supervised visual encoder trained with a representation objective. And the moment you give the generative model access to those stronger representations, whether through alignment or by building on top of them directly, it learns faster and generalizes better. That told me the representation was doing a lot of the heavy lifting the whole time.

So the way I'd put it is that a world model has really two separable jobs. One is to build a representation of state, something that captures what matters about the scene, the objects, the agent, their relationships, in a compact and predictable form. The other is to model dynamics in that space, how the state evolves under actions and over time. Generation, rendering back into pixels, is a third thing that's useful for humans to look at and useful for some downstream tasks, but it shouldn't be the backbone. I'd rather predict in a latent space where the next state is actually predictable, and then decode only when I need to.

The hard open question, and I think it's a genuinely open one, is what the right representation space is. Should it be something learned purely from visual self-supervision? Should it be grounded in language, because language already encodes a lot of abstraction that humans have refined over a long time? Or should it be more spatial, more 3D-aware, more like how a navigating animal represents its surroundings? My intuition is that today's vision representations are still too "flat." They're very good at semantics and categories, and not nearly good enough at space, geometry, and persistence over time. And those are exactly the capabilities a world model needs. So I'd say representation isn't a component you bolt on. It's really the design question, and the architecture should be organized around it rather than around the decoder.

r001.rationale: The response calls representation where the world model’s “world” lives and says the architecture should be organized around it, making it the central component.

r002.rationale: The response describes predicting in a latent space and decoding it into pixels, but does not say the shared representation can be decoded into different output modalities.

astra-6.text:
I think representation is a central question, because a world model doesn’t necessarily need to predict every detail of the world. It needs to capture the information that matters for understanding what is happening and what could happen next.

Imagine a robot trying to pick up a cup. The exact texture of the table may be less important than the cup’s position, its geometry, and how it will move when the robot touches it. A useful representation should preserve those relationships. But you also have to be careful: if you discard information too early, you may remove something that becomes important for a different task.

So I would think about representation and prediction together. What space are you predicting in? What information does that space preserve? Can it support different actions and different possible futures? Those questions shape the architecture itself.

The challenge is to learn a representation that makes prediction manageable while remaining rich enough to support decisions. A model can generate something that looks plausible without necessarily capturing the structure you need to act in the world.

r001.rationale: The response calls representation “a central question” and says it shapes the architecture, but does not identify it as the most important component.

r002.rationale: The response discusses what information a representation should preserve, but does not describe a shared underlying representation decoded into different output modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think representation is really at the center of a world model. We often focus on the architecture—whether it’s a transformer, for example—but the more fundamental question is: what is the model representing, and what should it predict?

If you predict every pixel, you spend a lot of capacity modeling details that may not matter for understanding or acting in the world. But if your representation is too abstract, you may throw away information that becomes important later. So there’s a tension: you want to preserve the structure of the world while making the prediction problem tractable.

For me, the interesting question is how to learn that representation together with the dynamics. What aspects of a scene persist? What changes when an agent takes an action? A useful representation should make those relationships easier to learn. In that sense, representation isn’t just an encoder you attach to a world model. It helps define what kind of world model you can build.

r001.rationale: The response puts representation “at the center” of a world model and calls it more fundamental than the architecture.

r002.rationale: It discusses what a representation should preserve and predict, but does not describe a shared representation that can be decoded into different output modalities.
